practice: repeat create and save a new project with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. record and stop what you will learn: complete record and stop independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: r starts recording. space stops recording or playback. connect the microphone and reduce background noise. press r once and speak a short practice sentence. press space to stop. press ctrl+s to save the project. what should happen: recording feedback and a changing time position. if that does not happen: stop before trying again. check the selected input device and whether another application controls the microphone. practice: repeat record and stop with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. play and navigate what you will learn: complete play and navigate independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: space plays or stops. p pauses or resumes. home moves to the track start. end moves to the track end. press home. press space and listen from the beginning. press p to pause at a point you want to inspect. press p again to continue or space to stop. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: confirm that an audio track exists and the audacity window is active. practice: repeat play and navigate with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. advanced how-tos select and delete unwanted audio what you will learn: complete select and delete unwanted audio independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard commands: shift+right arrow or shift+left arrow extends a selection in small steps. delete removes the confirmed selection. ctrl+z undoes. press ctrl+s to protect the project. move playback near the unwanted sound and stop. hold shift while using an arrow key to extend the selection. use audacityâ€™s selection toolbar or screen-reader feedback to verify start and end times. press delete, then listen across the edit. press ctrl+z immediately if the wrong audio was removed. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: undo and create a smaller selection. never delete an unverified range. practice: repeat select and delete unwanted audio with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. record a second track what you will learn: complete record a second track independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard command: shift+r starts recording on a new track in current audacity versions. save the project and move to the intended start time. press shift+r. record the second part and press space to stop. use track navigation and solo or mute controls to review tracks separately. save again. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: undo the new recording and confirm audacityâ€™s recording preference and active track. practice: repeat record a second track with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. export an mp3 or wav file what you will learn: complete export an mp3 or wav file independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: use alt+f to open file, then choose export audio. press ctrl+s to save the editable project. open file and choose export audio. choose mp3 for a smaller listening copy or wav for higher-quality uncompressed audio. select the destination and enter a new filename. review format settings and activate export. open the exported file and verify its duration and sound. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: keep the project open. check the destination, filename, format, and any error dialog. practice: repeat export an mp3 or wav file with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. apply an effect safely what you will learn: complete apply an effect safely independently with keyboard or screen-reader feedback. before you begin: open the relevant application or device screen and use a fictional, public, or nonprivate practice item. exactly how to do it keyboard approach: select audio, open the effect menu with alt+c in many audacity versions, and choose an effect by name. save a backup project. select only the audio that should change. open the effect menu and choose the effect. preview it when available. apply it, listen again, and use ctrl+z if the result is worse. what should happen: the intended item, setting, or result is available and can be verified before you continue. if that does not happen: cancel the dialog rather than accepting settings you do not understand. practice: repeat apply an effect safely with a second safe practice item, then explain the commands you used. quick command list r: record shift+r: record a new track space: play or stop p: pause or resume home / end: start / end ctrl+s: save project ctrl+z: undo delete: remove selected audio return to manuals

entries.text: accessible job search screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual accessible job search screen reader manual keyboard-first employment skills independent self-study guide for finding and applying for work all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches an independent, accessible workflow for finding jobs, evaluating postings, preparing resumes, completing online applications, requesting application-process accommodations when needed, and interviewing with common digital tools. platforms: the main desktop examples use windows with jaws, nvda, or narrator, but the workflow also applies to voiceover and talkback. dedicated sections cover linkedin and indeed, while company career sites are treated as variable third-party systems. legal scope: the accommodation section provides general u.s. employment-access information and practical communication guidance, not individualized legal advice. how to use this manual build your resume and reusable application information before starting a live application. open every job posting in a separate tab or save the link so you can return to it while applying. read the entire job description before investing time in the application. keep a private application tracker with employer, role, date, link, status, contact, and next action. use headings, landmarks, form controls, and browser find rather than only tab through long pages. when an application is inaccessible, document the barrier and use the employer accommodation/contact route rather than repeatedly fighting the same control. never pay an employer or recruiter to apply, receive equipment, cash a check, buy gift cards, or release a job offer. before interviews, test the meeting platform, microphone, camera if used, screen reader, headphones, and any requested accommodation. table of contents part 1 - build a job-search workspace part 2 - prepare an accessible resume part 3 - resume file formats and uploads part 4 - read a job posting efficiently part 5 - evaluate qualifications and essential functions part 6 - search on linkedin with a screen reader part 7 - apply on linkedin part 8 - search and apply on indeed part 9 - company career sites and ats systems part 10 - online application forms part 11 - dropdowns, date pickers, autocomplete, and custom controls part 12 - resume parsing and re-entering work history part 13 - cover letters and application questions part 14 - assessments and timed tests part 15 - requesting an application accommodation part 16 - disability disclosure and interview boundaries part 17 - job-search scams part 18 - email and recruiter communication part 19 - interview scheduling part 20 - zoom, teams, and video interviews part 21 - interview preparation with a screen reader part 22 - after the interview part 23 - application tracking and follow-up part 24 - mobile job search part 25 - troubleshooting inaccessible applications part 26 - independent practice course part 27 - quick reference checklists part 28 - official resources part 1 - build a job-search workspace create a folder named job search with subfolders for resume, cover letters, applications, and interview notes. keep one master resume and create role-specific copies from it. keep a plain-text file with frequently requested information: employment dates, supervisor names, addresses, phone numbers, education dates, certifications, and references. keep a private application tracker. do not store social security numbers, passwords, full banking details, or identity documents in the tracker. use a professional email address that you check regularly. 1.1 create an application tracker what you will learn: track jobs so you know what you applied to and what comes next. before you begin: open excel, google sheets, or another accessible spreadsheet. exactly how to do it create columns for employer, job title, job id, location, date found, date applied, source/link, contact, status, follow-up date, and notes. enter one practice job. save the tracker in your job search folder. after every application, update the status immediately. what should happen: you can answer â€œwhat have i applied to?â€ without searching your email. if that does not happen: if a spreadsheet is cumbersome, use a simple word table or structured text list instead. practice: track three practice postings. part 2 - prepare an accessible resume use real word headings for major sections such as summary, skills, experience, and education. use simple one-column reading order. prefer standard fonts and ordinary text over text boxes, floating shapes, icons, charts, or infographic skill bars. use actual bullet lists for achievements. write employer, job title, dates, and accomplishments as text that reads logically linearly. do not use color alone to communicate meaning. use meaningful link text for linkedin/portfolio links. run word accessibility checker before exporting. 2.1 check resume reading order what you will learn: make sure the resume reads correctly from top to bottom. before you begin: open the resume in word. exactly how to do it press ctrl+home. use ctrl+down arrow or your screen reader reading commands to move through the document. listen for each section in the intended order. use the screen reader heading list to verify section headings. use tab to identify hyperlinks and confirm their text is meaningful. run review > check accessibility and fix relevant issues. what should happen: the resume makes sense without visual position cues. if that does not happen: if information is announced out of order, remove text boxes/columns and rebuild that area in normal paragraphs or a simple table. practice: read your resume from top to bottom without using sighted layout cues. part 3 - resume file formats and uploads task how docx usually best when the employer explicitly requests word or when an ats parses word documents well. pdf useful when you want layout preserved; export from an accessible source and verify the pdf has real selectable/tagged text. plain text useful as a fallback for copy/paste fields; not usually the primary polished resume. image/scanned pdf avoid. it may be unreadable and difficult for ats/screen readers. 3.1 upload a resume reliably what you will learn: use a file-upload control without losing your place. before you begin: keep the resume in a known folder with a clear filename. exactly how to do it focus the upload resume or choose file button. press enter or space. in the file chooser, press ctrl+l if needed to type the folder path, or use the normal file explorer navigation. find the resume filename. press enter. return to the application and listen for the uploaded filename or success message. if the site parsed your resume into fields, review every parsed field before submission. what should happen: the correct filename is attached and the application recognizes it. if that does not happen: if the filename is not announced, inspect nearby status text or re-focus the upload control. do not assume the upload worked. practice: upload a disposable resume copy to a safe form or practice environment. part 4 - read a job posting efficiently 4.1 build a posting summary what you will learn: extract the facts you need before applying. before you begin: open the job posting. exactly how to do it use h or your screen reader heading-navigation command to find the job title and major sections. use browser find (ctrl+f) for terms such as salary, location, remote, qualifications, required, preferred, schedule, travel, clearance, license, benefits, and accommodation. read the entire responsibilities and qualifications sections. write down the job id/requisition number. copy the posting link into your tracker. note the closing date if one is listed. what should happen: you can summarize the job without rereading the entire page. if that does not happen: if headings are poor, use browser find and landmarks/form controls ins

entries.text: adobe acrobat and accessible pdf screen reader manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual adobe acrobat and accessible pdf screen reader manual reading, navigating, creating, and checking pdfs independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual adobe acrobat reader accessibility features purpose: this manual teaches how to read, navigate, complete, save, print, and evaluate pdfs with a screen reader, and how to recognize when a pdf needs ocr or accessibility remediation. reader versus acrobat pro: adobe acrobat reader is primarily for reading, forms, comments, and everyday pdf use. acrobat pro adds authoring and remediation tools such as accessibility checking, automatic tagging, reading order, and advanced tag repair. reference platform: main procedures focus on current acrobat/acrobat reader on windows. separate sections cover macos/voiceover and braille. how to use this manual a screen reader can only read what the pdf exposes as text and structure. a tagged pdf is usually easier to navigate than an untagged pdf. an image-only scanned pdf may contain no readable text until ocr is performed. use ctrl+f for text search, ctrl+0/1/2/3/4/5 for common view/reflow commands as supported, and ctrl+shift+5 for current-document reading settings. do not confuse adobe read out loud with your screen reader; read out loud is adobe text-to-speech, not a substitute for accessible tagging. for long untagged pdfs, reader may take time to analyze reading order. when a pdf reads badly, test whether the problem is the document before changing global screen-reader settings. table of contents part 1 - what a pdf is part 2 - acrobat reader vs acrobat pro part 3 - open a pdf and learn the window part 4 - page navigation part 5 - text reading and selection part 6 - search part 7 - links and bookmarks part 8 - forms part 9 - comments and annotations part 10 - saving, printing, and exporting part 11 - tagged vs untagged pdfs part 12 - scanned/image-only pdfs and ocr part 13 - reading order and document structure part 14 - reflow and reading settings part 15 - accessibility setup assistant part 16 - read out loud part 17 - creating and checking accessible pdfs in acrobat pro part 18 - fixing reading order in acrobat pro part 19 - tables, lists, headings, language, and alt text part 20 - narrator part 21 - nvda part 22 - jaws part 23 - voiceover part 24 - braille displays part 25 - pdf security and signatures part 26 - troubleshooting part 27 - independent practice course part 28 - quick reference part 29 - official adobe resources part 1 - what a pdf is pdf means portable document format. a pdf can preserve page appearance, but visual appearance does not guarantee accessibility. text pdf: contains selectable/extractable text. tagged pdf: contains a logical structure tree identifying headings, paragraphs, lists, tables, figures, links, and reading order. untagged pdf: may contain real text but little or no structural information. scanned/image-only pdf: may be only pictures of pages until ocr adds a text layer. form pdf: can contain interactive text fields, checkboxes, radio buttons, buttons, and signatures. part 2 - acrobat reader vs acrobat pro product typical accessibility role acrobat reader read pdfs, use forms, comments, accessibility preferences, read out loud, save/print common pdfs. acrobat pro includes reader functions plus accessibility checking, tagging/remediation, reading order, ocr and advanced document repair. rule of thumb: if you only need to consume a pdf, reader may be enough. if you must repair or certify pdf accessibility, acrobat pro is normally required. part 3 - open a pdf and learn the window 3.1 open a local pdf what you will learn: open a known file in acrobat/reader. before you begin: know the pdf location. exactly how to do it press ctrl+o. navigate the windows open dialog to the pdf. press enter. wait for the document to load. press tab and shift+tab slowly to identify toolbar and document controls. use your screen reader reading command in the document area. what should happen: the pdf opens and accessible content is exposed to the screen reader. if that does not happen: if the screen reader announces only image, blank, or very little content, the pdf may be scanned or poorly structured. practice: open one known accessible pdf. browser pdfs: pdfs may open in chrome or edge instead of acrobat. download/open the file in acrobat when you need adobe-specific accessibility preferences or pro remediation tools. part 4 - page navigation task command next page page down or ctrl+page down depending view/context previous page page up or ctrl+page up depending view/context first page home/ctrl+home depending focus last page end/ctrl+end depending focus go to page use page-number field or navigation control; ctrl+shift+n is commonly used in acrobat for go to page 4.1 go to a specific page what you will learn: reach a page without reading every page before it. before you begin: open a multi-page pdf. exactly how to do it move to the page-number control in the toolbar, or invoke the go to page command available in your acrobat version. type the page number. press enter. use the screen reader to verify the page heading/text. what should happen: the requested page becomes active. if that does not happen: if the printed page number differs from the pdf page index, use bookmarks/headings/search for better orientation. practice: jump to three different pages. part 5 - text reading and selection 5.1 read pdf text with your screen reader what you will learn: read text using the screen reader rather than acrobat tts. before you begin: the pdf exposes selectable text. exactly how to do it move focus into the document pane. use your screen reader say all/read commands. use line, word, heading, link, and table commands when the pdf is tagged. stop speech with the screen reader stop-speech command when needed. what should happen: the screen reader follows the pdf text and document structure. if that does not happen: if reading order jumps unpredictably, the pdf may be untagged or incorrectly tagged. practice: read one page continuously, then navigate by structure. 5.2 select and copy text what you will learn: copy a short accessible passage. before you begin: use a pdf that allows copying. exactly how to do it move the screen reader/caret to the desired text. select with shift plus navigation keys or the screen reader selection mechanism. press ctrl+c. paste into a harmless text editor with ctrl+v to confirm. what should happen: the selected text copies in a sensible order. if that does not happen: if copied text is scrambled or unavailable, the pdf may use inaccessible encoding, permissions, or image-only pages. practice: copy one sentence. part 6 - search 6.1 find text what you will learn: locate a word in a long pdf. before you begin: pdf contains searchable text. exactly how to do it press ctrl+f. type a word or phrase. press enter. use the find next/previous controls or enter/shift+enter as available. press escape when finished. what should happen: acrobat moves to matching text. if that does not happen: if a visible word cannot be found, the page may be image-only or text extraction may be broken. practice: search for three terms. part 7 - links and bookmarks 7.1 use pdf bookmarks what you will learn: navigate a structured long document. before you begin: the pdf contains bookmarks. exactly how to do it open the bookmarks side panel with the acrobat navigation-pane controls. use arrow keys through bookmarks. press enter on the desired bookmark. return to the document pane and read from the new location. what should happen: the pdf jumps to the bookmarked section. if that does not happen: if no bookmarks exist, use headings/search/page navigation. practice: navigate to three bookmarks. 7.2 activate a link what you will learn: open a link deliberately. before you begin: focus a link in the pdf. e

entries.text: ai fundamentals and responsible use manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible artificial intelligence foundations ai fundamentals and responsible use manual independent self-study guide for responsible, accessible ai use. all manuals table of contents website practice procedures ai lessons purpose: this manual explains artificial intelligence from the beginning and teaches how to use ai tools responsibly. it assumes no prior technical knowledge. who this is for: students, employees, job seekers, independent learners, screen-reader and braille users, and anyone who wants to understand ai before relying on it. core principle: ai can be useful without being authoritative. treat ai output as assistance that may require verification, not as automatic truth. responsible-use foundation: the guide reflects current responsible-ai principles from nist and unesco, including risk management, transparency, fairness, privacy, human oversight, and awareness of generative-ai-specific risks. how to use this manual read parts 1 through 8 before using ai for important work; they establish the concepts needed to judge ai output. practice with low-risk tasks first, such as brainstorming, rewriting your own text, or generating study questions. do not paste confidential, private, regulated, or employer/client data into an ai system unless the relevant policy and service terms permit it. verify important factual claims using trustworthy independent sources. keep the human decision-maker responsible for important decisions. use ai to support accessibility and independence, but check outputs that describe images, documents, people, or environments. when an ai tool cannot provide sources, treat precise factual claims with extra caution. keep records of significant ai use when school, workplace, legal, or organizational policy requires disclosure. table of contents part 1 - what artificial intelligence is part 2 - ai, machine learning, deep learning, and generative ai part 3 - how generative ai produces an answer part 4 - large language models and tokens part 5 - training data, context, and knowledge limits part 6 - what ai is good at part 7 - what ai is not good at part 8 - hallucinations and confident errors part 9 - prompting fundamentals part 10 - better prompt structure part 11 - follow-up questions and iteration part 12 - sources, search, and grounding part 13 - verification and fact-checking part 14 - privacy and sensitive information part 15 - security and prompt injection part 16 - bias, fairness, and representation part 17 - copyright, attribution, and ownership part 18 - education and academic integrity part 19 - workplace and professional use part 20 - high-stakes decisions part 21 - accessibility and assistive technology part 22 - images, audio, video, and deepfakes part 23 - ai agents and automated actions part 24 - responsible human oversight part 25 - a practical responsible-use framework part 26 - troubleshooting poor ai results part 27 - practice course part 28 - quick reference checklists part 29 - official resources part 1 - what artificial intelligence is artificial intelligence is a broad term for computer systems designed to perform tasks that people associate with intelligent behavior, such as recognizing patterns, understanding language, generating content, making predictions, recommending actions, or controlling devices. ai is not one single technology. an ai system may be narrow and specialized, such as spam detection or speech recognition. an ai system may generate new content, such as text, images, audio, video, or code. an ai system may recommend or rank options without generating visible content. ai output is produced by a system, not by an independent human expert reviewing your situation. important distinction: a system can produce a fluent answer without having human experience, personal awareness, or guaranteed understanding of the real-world situation. part 2 - ai, machine learning, deep learning, and generative ai topic what to remember artificial intelligence (ai) the broad field of systems that perform tasks associated with intelligent behavior. machine learning (ml) a way of building systems that learn patterns from data rather than relying only on hand-written rules. deep learning machine learning using multi-layer neural networks; widely used in speech, vision, and modern generative systems. generative ai ai that creates new content such as text, images, audio, video, or code. large language model (llm) a generative model trained to work with language and related symbolic information. relationship: generative ai is part of ai. many current generative systems use deep-learning methods, but not every ai system is generative. part 3 - how generative ai produces an answer a generative model receives your input, combines it with the conversation/context and system instructions, and predicts a useful continuation. for language models, this involves predicting sequences of tokens. the answer is generated at request time; it is not normally retrieved as one complete prewritten paragraph. generation is influenced by the prompt, prior conversation, system instructions, model design, and available tools/data. a fluent answer can contain invented details because plausible language is not the same as verified truth. different prompts can lead to different answers to the same underlying question. mental model: think of generative ai as a powerful pattern-and-language engine with reasoning capabilities that still needs verification, not as an infallible encyclopedia. part 4 - large language models and tokens large language models process text in smaller units called tokens. a token can be a whole word, part of a word, punctuation, or another unit. long conversations consume context space. the model may pay less attention to older details when a conversation becomes very long. exact token counts depend on the model and tokenizer. giving clear, relevant context is usually more useful than giving large amounts of unrelated text. practical lesson: if an ai starts forgetting instructions in a long conversation, restate the key requirements or begin a clean conversation with a concise summary. part 5 - training data, context, and knowledge limits models learn statistical patterns during training. at use time, a model may also receive current context, uploaded files, retrieved information, or web/search results if the product supports those tools. training data is not the same thing as a live database. a model may not know that a fact has changed unless it has current retrieval/search access. a model may mix accurate information with outdated or incorrect information. an answer about current laws, prices, schedules, public figures, software versions, or news should be verified with current sources. uploaded documents and connected data can improve relevance but increase privacy responsibility. current information rule: for time-sensitive questions, ask the ai to verify with current sources when the product can browse or search. part 6 - what ai is good at brainstorming ideas and alternatives. explaining a concept at different reading levels. summarizing text you provide. rewriting your own material for clarity, tone, or structure. generating practice questions or study aids. creating outlines, checklists, templates, and first drafts. classifying or organizing information with human review. translating or simplifying material, with verification for important use. helping with code, formulas, and troubleshooting when results are tested. accessibility support such as describing visual structure or converting information into a more usable format. best use pattern: ai is often strongest when the user can evaluate the result or verify it independently. part 7 - what ai is not good at guaranteeing that a factual statement is true. knowing unstated facts about a person, event, image, or organization. replacing professional judgment in hi

entries.text: android talkback manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual android talkback manual touch gestures, navigation, typing, and apps independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual google android accessibility help - talkback purpose: this manual teaches android with talkback from the beginning. it explains physical orientation, touch exploration, navigation, typing, system gestures, web browsing, talkback settings, braille input/output, external keyboards, security, troubleshooting, and independent practice. device differences: android phones and tablets vary by manufacturer. pixel, samsung galaxy, motorola, oneplus, and other devices may place buttons differently or rename settings. the talkback concepts and core gestures are consistent, but exact menus can differ. current reference: the guide is aligned with current android accessibility help, including android 16-era talkback features and talkback 16.2 keyboard/braille changes. how to use this manual work through the first gesture sections slowly. talkback changes how ordinary touch works. touching an item normally speaks it; activating it usually requires a double-tap. one-finger swipes generally move talkback focus. two-finger gestures generally scroll or perform system navigation when gesture navigation is in use. use the built-in talkback tutorial and practice area whenever a gesture feels unreliable. on devices that support multi-finger gestures, a three-finger tap opens the talkback menu. reading controls change what an up/down swipe navigates: characters, words, headings, controls, and more. braille support is built into talkback. brailleback is not required for current supported braille displays. when typing with the talkback braille keyboard, normal talkback gestures are temporarily replaced by braille-keyboard gestures. never change several talkback settings at once while learning. change one setting, test it, and keep or reverse it. table of contents part 1 - what talkback is part 2 - physical orientation and android device types part 3 - turn talkback on and off part 4 - talkback tutorial and practice part 5 - explore by touch part 6 - core one-finger navigation part 7 - activate, long-press, and scroll part 8 - home, back, overview, notifications, and quick settings part 9 - talkback menu and reading controls part 10 - home screen and app drawer part 11 - notifications part 12 - quick settings part 13 - text entry with gboard part 14 - text editing and selection part 15 - voice typing and google assistant part 16 - chrome and web navigation part 17 - messages and email part 18 - phone and video calls part 19 - talkback settings and speech part 20 - hide screen and privacy features part 21 - talkback braille keyboard part 22 - refreshable braille displays part 23 - external keyboard and enhanced keymap part 24 - files, sharing, and downloads part 25 - device security and privacy part 26 - manufacturer differences part 27 - troubleshooting part 28 - independent practice course part 29 - quick reference gestures part 30 - official google resources part 1 - what talkback is talkback is android's built-in screen reader. it speaks or displays in braille what is focused, describes controls and alerts, and changes the touch interface so a blind or low-vision user can navigate independently. focus: the item talkback is currently describing. explore by touch: drag one finger around the screen and talkback speaks what is under the finger. swipe navigation: move focus in a predictable sequence without needing to know where items are visually. activation: after focusing an item, double-tap anywhere with one finger to activate it. reading controls: change the navigation unit used by up/down swipes. talkback menu: quick access to settings, voice commands, screen search, hide/show screen, and context actions. braille: talkback supports both an onscreen braille keyboard and connected refreshable braille displays. part 2 - physical orientation and android device types important: there is no single physical android layout. always identify your exact device model before memorizing button locations. most modern phones have a flat touchscreen on the front, one or more cameras near the top, and physical side buttons. common side buttons include power/side key and volume up/down. their side and vertical order vary by manufacturer. usb-c is the standard charging/data connector on most current android phones and tablets and is usually on the bottom edge. some tablets place usb-c on a side edge depending on orientation. some devices use on-screen gesture navigation; others use a three-button navigation bar with back, home, and overview/recents. foldable phones may have multiple displays and hinge-dependent layouts. 2.1 identify your device before learning gestures what you will learn: create a reliable physical map of your own phone/tablet. before you begin: have the device powered on and safely held. exactly how to do it find the screen: the large smooth glass surface on the front. find the power/side key and press it briefly once to hear whether the screen locks/wakes. find volume up and volume down by pressing each once and listening for the volume change. locate the charging port by touch without inserting a cable blindly at an angle. ask settings > about phone/tablet for the exact manufacturer and model name if you do not know it. write down the exact model and button layout in your own notes. what should happen: you have a model-specific physical map instead of relying on generic assumptions. if that does not happen: if you cannot identify a control safely, use the manufacturer's official hardware guide for that exact model. practice: locate each physical control three times with the screen off. part 3 - turn talkback on and off 3.1 turn talkback on in settings what you will learn: enable talkback using the standard android settings path. before you begin: the device is already set up and you can access settings. exactly how to do it open settings. open accessibility. open talkback. turn use talkback on. confirm the permission/confirmation prompt. listen to talkback begin speaking. what should happen: talkback starts and touch behavior changes. if that does not happen: menu names vary by manufacturer. use settings search for talkback if necessary. practice: turn talkback on and enter the tutorial. 3.2 configure the talkback shortcut what you will learn: make it possible to toggle talkback without navigating settings. before you begin: talkback is on. exactly how to do it open settings > accessibility > talkback. open talkback shortcut. turn the shortcut on. follow the device-specific instructions for the offered shortcut method. test the shortcut once to turn talkback off, then use it again to turn talkback on. what should happen: you can toggle talkback using the configured accessibility shortcut. if that does not happen: the shortcut varies by device and android version. do not assume one universal button combination. practice: toggle talkback off and back on without opening settings. 3.3 use google assistant to toggle talkback what you will learn: use voice control when assistant is already configured. before you begin: google assistant/gemini voice activation is available on the device. exactly how to do it say hey google. say turn on talkback or turn off talkback. wait for the change to complete. what should happen: talkback changes state by voice command. if that does not happen: if assistant is not configured, use settings or the accessibility shortcut instead. practice: use voice to turn talkback on once. android 16 keyboard option: google documents an android 16 external-keyboard shortcut for talkback using the action key + alt + t. the action key depends on the keyboard, such as windows key on a windows keyboard or command on a entries.text: braillenote touch plus manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual braillenote touch plus manual braille-first android productivity independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches the braillenote touch plus from the beginning. it assumes no prior experience and provides physical orientation, exact braille-keyboard commands, expected speech/braille feedback, troubleshooting, practice, and independence checks. current reference: humanware's current support page lists braillenote touch plus user guide version 6. the command model in this guide follows humanware's current keysoft documentation and current support materials. important product note: the braillenote touch plus is an android-based braille notetaker with humanware's keysoft accessibility layer. it can also work as a braille display for a computer or mobile device through braille terminal. how to use this manual first learn the physical controls and keysoft navigation pattern before using email, web, or third-party apps. main menu: home button or space with dots 1-2-3-4-5-6. next item: next thumb key or space. previous item: previous thumb key or backspace. activate selected item: enter (dot 8) or a cursor-routing key. back/exit current screen: back button or space with e. contextual help: space with h. context menu: space with m or press and hold recent apps. braille panning: left and right thumb keys. use first-letter navigation in lists and menus whenever keysoft supports it. do not change android accessibility settings casually; keysoft is the accessibility layer that makes the touch plus usable. before connecting the touch plus as an external braille display, first pair/connect it, then configure the host screen reader, then test braille output, input, and routing. table of contents part 1 - what the braillenote touch plus is the braillenote touch plus combines a touchscreen android tablet, keysoft applications, speech, a 32-cell refreshable braille display, and a removable physical braille-keyboard cover. keysoft main menu: the primary accessible home screen. keyword: word processing. keymail: email. keylist: contacts. keyplan: calendar/planner. keyfiles: file manager. easyreader plus: accessible book-reading app. google chrome: web browser. braille terminal: turns the touch plus into an external braille display for another device. all applications: access to installed android and google play apps. part 2 - physical orientation 2.1 top face place the device flat with the touchscreen and braille display facing up and the seven front-edge buttons closest to you. the touchscreen occupies the upper portion of the top face. directly below the touchscreen is the 32-cell refreshable braille display. above each braille cell is a cursor-routing key. pressing a routing key moves the cursor or activates an item depending on context. internal stereo speakers are positioned to the left and right of the braille cells. an internal microphone is located to the right of the braille display, below the right speaker. the removable braille keyboard cover sits over the touchscreen when attached and provides perkins-style braille input. 2.2 front edge - seven buttons, left to right position control 1 previous thumb key 2 left thumb key 3 triangle back button 4 round home button 5 square recent apps button 6 right thumb key 7 next thumb key front-edge functions: previous/next move through items; left/right pan braille. back returns to the previous screen. home returns to keysoft main menu. recent apps shows running apps; press and hold it for the context menu. 2.3 left edge - top to bottom location control near top corner usb-c port for charging and computer connection below usb-c green led indicator below led oval power button below power volume up button below volume up volume down button 2.4 right edge - top to bottom location control near top corner microphone / line-in jack below microphone jack headphone / audio-out jack below headphone jack action button for recording, camera snapshots, and play/stop in supported contexts 2.5 rear edge - left to right location port near left corner full-size usb port for flash drives and other supported usb storage/devices next sdhc card slot next high-resolution video output port for external display/tv rightmost braille-keyboard-cover connector safety: do not force usb, sd, or keyboard-cover connectors. eject removable storage through keysoft before physically removing it. part 3 - entries.text: brailliant bi x manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual brailliant bi x manual braille display commands and independent operation independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches the humanware brailliant bi x series from the beginning. it covers the bi 20x and bi 40x, including physical orientation, keysoft lite, reading and editing, online libraries, terminal mode, connections to computers and mobile devices, troubleshooting, practice, and quick-reference commands. current reference: humanware's current support pages list user guide version 2.6 and firmware version 2.6.0 build 5120 for the bi 20x and bi 40x. model difference: the bi 20x has 20 braille cells and no six-key command cluster. the bi 40x has 40 braille cells plus six configurable command keys, three on each side of the display. how to use this manual place the device flat with the braille cells closest to you. use previous and next thumb keys to move through menus. use left and right thumb keys to pan braille. press enter (dot 8) or any routing key to activate the selected item. press space+e to go back. press home or space+dots 1-2-3-4-5-6 to return to main menu. press space+h for help and space+m for the context menu. use first-letter navigation in keysoft lite lists and menus. terminal mode is different from keysoft lite: once connected to a host screen reader, host-screen-reader commands take precedence. connection rule: pair/connect first, configure the host screen reader second, then test output, input, and routing. before removing usb/sd storage, use enter+e to eject it safely. table of contents part 1 - what the brailliant bi x is part 2 - physical orientation part 3 - charging, power, and battery part 4 - core keysoft lite navigation part 5 - help, context menu, and status part 6 - braille profiles and speech part 7 - physical orientation 2.1 top face - both models place the brailliant flat with the braille cells closest to you. the front section of the top face contains the 20 or 40 braille cells. immediately above each cell is a routing key. in text editing, a routing key moves the cursor to that cell. in menus, a routing key activates the selected item. two space bars are positioned for the thumbs. farther away from you is the perkins-style braille keyboard. under the left hand: dots 1, 2, 3 and backspace (dot 7). dot 1 is under the left index finger; backspace is under the left little finger. under the right hand: dots 4, 5, 6 and enter (dot 8). dot 4 is under the right index finger; enter is under the right little finger. 2.2 bi 40x command keys only the bi 40x has six command keys around the braille display. left side of the display, from back to front: c1, c2, c3. right side of the display, from back to front: c4, c5, c6. current default functions include c1 previous item, c2 pan left, c3 next item, c4 switch language profile, c5 pan right, and c6 start auto-scroll. these command keys can be reassigned in user settings. 2.3 front edge - both models position control far left previous thumb key left-center left thumb key center round home button right-center right thumb key far right next thumb key use: previous/next move through menu items. left/right pan braille. home returns to main menu and exits terminal mode. 2.4 left edge - front to back location control / port front usb-a port behind usb-a power button behind power green status led back usb-c port for charging and usb host connection 2.5 right edge - front to back volume buttons. 3.5 mm audio jack. on the bi 40x, the right edge/top area also includes speaker hardware; audio features depend on current firmware/function. 2.6 bi 20x rear edge the bi 20x has an sd-card slot on the rear edge near the left side. the bi 40x does not use this bi 20x rear sd-card layout. part 3 - charging, power, and battery 3.1 charge the brailliant what you will learn: connect power without forcing the connector. before you begin: use the included usb-c cable and a suitable usb power adapter. exactly how to do it locate the usb-c port at the back end of the left edge. insert the usb-c plug gently. connect the other end to the power adapter. plug the adapter into ac power. allow the battery to charge. what should happen: the status led/braille status indicates charging. if that does not happen: if the device does not charge, try the included cable/adapter and a different outlet. practice: locate usb-c and connect/disconnect it correctly. 3.2 power on and check battery what you will learn: start the device and verify charge. before you begin: battery has some charge. exactly how to do it press and hold the power button for about two seconds. wait for keysoft lite to start. press enter+p. read/listen to the battery level. what should happen: main menu appears and the battery percentage/status is reported. if that does not happen: if nothing happens, connect power and retry. practice: power on and report battery level. firmware update warning: humanware states that units still on firmware 1.x must first install version 2.0 manually before updating to later firmware. part 4 - part 35 - independent practice course part 36 - quick reference part 37 - official openai resources part 1 - what chatgpt is chatgpt is an ai assistant from openai. it can work with natural-language instructions and, depending on the experience and plan, can search the web, analyze files and images, generate images, run data analysis, use voice, organize work in projects, use connected apps, perform deep research, schedule tasks, and complete longer multi-step work. chatgpt generates responses from the conversation and available tools/context. it can make mistakes, including confident factual errors. it does not automatically know that information has changed unless current information is retrieved. different plans and workspaces may expose different models, tools, limits, and permissions. an organization's administrator may restrict plugins, apps, work, file use, browsing, or data settings. part 2 - chat, work, and codex experience best use chat fast conversational help, questions, brainstorming, search, files, images, voice, and everyday assistance. work longer multi-step work and finished deliverables; can use files, apps, browsers, tasks, and approvals when available. codex software-development experience for writing/debugging code, repositories, tests, terminals, and developer workflows. availability: chat is the default experience. work is available to eligible paid plans and may be controlled by workspace administrators. codex availability depends on the product surface and plan. important ui change: older chatgpt instructions may refer to canvas. current writing and coding workflows are delivered through writing blocks, code blocks, work, and other current tools instead. part 3 - open chatgpt and start a chat 3.1 start a new chat on the web what you will learn: open a clean conversation. before you begin: use an up-to-date supported browser. exactly how to do it press ctrl+l or alt+d to focus the browser address bar. type chatgpt.com. press enter. sign in if required. find and activate new chat using tab/shift+tab, screen-reader button navigation, or the sidebar. move to the message/prompt edit field. type a simple question such as: explain what a spreadsheet is in three sentences. activate send or press enter when the edit field uses enter to submit. what should happen: a new assistant response appears in the conversation. if that does not happen: if enter inserts a new line instead of sending, locate and activate the send button. if focus is lost, use edit-field navigation to return to the prompt. practice: start three low-risk chats on different topics. 3.2 continue a conversation what you will learn: ask a follow-up without repeating all context. before you begin: a response is already present. exactly how to do it return to the prompt edit field. ask a follow-up that clearly refers to the prior answer, such as: give me an example. send the message. read the new response. ask one more follow-up that changes the format, such as: turn that into a checklist. what should happen: chatgpt uses the existing conversation context. if that does not happen: if it misunderstands what 'that' refers to, restate the subject explicitly. practice: use three follow-ups in one chat. part 4 - understand the chat interface sidebar/recents: previous chats and projects; exact names and ordering can change. new chat: begins a fresh conversation. conversation area: contains your messages, assistant responses, citations, widgets, files, and other results. prompt/message field: where you type or dictate the next request. attachment/plus controls: can expose file, image, search, study, or other tools depending on plan/device. model/mode or experience controls: can change the model, chat/work experience, temporary chat, or other behavior depending on current ui. profile/settings: account, personalization, data controls, notifications, apps/plugins, and other preferences. screen reader strategy: navigate by headings, buttons, edit fields, and landmarks instead of pressing tab through every element in a long conversation. part 5 - prompting fundamentals task how / what to know goal what do you want chatgpt to do? context what background is needed? constraints length, audience, tone, exclusions, date, platform, or other requirements. input text, file, data, problem, or question to work with. output paragraph, numbered steps, table, email, checklist, code, etc. verification ask for current sources or uncertainty when correctness matters. 5.1 write a strong basic prompt what you will learn: get a useful answer without unnecessary back-and-forth. before you begin: choose a harmless task. exactly how to do it state the goal first. add the audience or purpose. add only relevant context. magnification, browser zoom, color settings, and keyboard. confirm that focus is announced, controls have useful names, editing feedback is understandable, and essential tasks do not require a mouse. use descriptive headings, real lists, clear table headers, meaningful links, alternative text, sufficient contrast, and logical reading order. do not communicate meaning only through color or visual position. run the programâ€™s accessibility checker when available, but also perform a keyboard and screen-reader review. keep an original editable file before exporting pdf or converting formats. native and exchange formats libreoffice native formats odt for writer, ods for calc, and odp for impress preserve libreoffice editing features. microsoft exchange formats docx, xlsx, and pptx are often required by employers or instructors using microsoft 365. other formats csv carries plain spreadsheet data without formulas or formatting. pdf is useful for fixed-layout review but may be harder to edit and must be checked for accessibility. save the native version first. then save or download a separate exchange copy and review it in the receiving program whenever possible. jaws, narrator, and nvda interfaces vary by program and update. use tab and shift+tab for controls, arrow keys within menus and lists, enter or space to activate, alt or f10 for menus when supported, ctrl+s to save, ctrl+o to open, and ctrl+z to undo. listen for the current control name and state instead of memorizing screen position. jaws: use insert+t for the window title, insert+tab for focused-control information, and insert+1 for keyboard help. nvda: use nvda+t for the title, nvda+tab for focus, and nvda+1 for input help. narrator: use caps lock+t for the title and caps lock+1 for input learning. toggle scan mode only when the application or webpage requires it. browser-based editors may have their own screen-reader-support setting and keyboard shortcuts. read the current official help before description, formula result, note, and page or slide count. check fonts, spacing, page breaks, charts, animations, formulas, comments, and accessibility metadata. correct the native file and export again rather than repeatedly converting the same exchange copy. never promise perfect compatibility without testing the actual document in the receiving software. privacy, accounts, and sharing use entries.text: cybersecurity for screen reader users manual - accessible learning center skip to main content accessible learning center manual cybersecurity for screen reader users manual safer accounts, devices, browsing, and communication independent self-study guide all manuals table of contents start of manual purpose: this manual teaches practical cybersecurity to people who use screen readers, braille displays, keyboard navigation, or speech access. it assumes no technical security background. core approach: security decisions should not depend on seeing color, logos, icons, hover previews, or visual layout. this guide teaches verification methods that work through accessible text, keyboard commands, screen-reader information, known apps, saved bookmarks, typed addresses, and trusted contact methods. safety principle: urgency is not proof. a legitimate bank, employer, government agency, software company, or family member can be contacted independently. never let a message force you to use only the contact method inside that same message. how to use this manual work through the manual in order. the first sections establish habits used everywhere else. when a message is suspicious, do not click, reply, call the included number, or open the attachment just to investigate. use a known app, saved bookmark, typed website address, statement/card phone number, or trusted contact record to verify independently. treat passwords, recovery codes, one-time codes, passkeys, security questions, and remote-control access as credentials. keep software updated; security updates close known weaknesses. use a password manager and unique passwords where passwords are still required. turn on mfa; prefer passkeys or other phishing-resistant methods where available. if something goes wrong, act quickly: disconnect remote access, secure the account, change credentials, turn on mfa, scan/update devices, and contact the legitimate institution. table of contents part 1 - the four core cybersecurity habits part 2 - what phishing is part 3 - accessible sender verification part 4 - accessible link verification part 5 - suspicious attachments and downloads part 6 - passwords and password managers part 7 - mfa, authenticator apps, and security keys part 8 - passkeys part 9 - one-time codes and mfa fatigue part 10 - browser and website security warnings part 11 - email safety part 12 - text messages, calls, and voicemail scams part 13 - tech-support and remote-access scams part 14 - banking, payment, gift card, and refund scams part 15 - social media, dating, and impersonation scams part 16 - shopping, delivery, and subscription scams part 17 - software updates and safe apps part 18 - backups and ransomware resilience part 19 - public wi-fi, bluetooth, and device privacy part 20 - screen reader and braille privacy part 21 - account recovery and security alerts part 22 - what to do after a scam or account compromise part 23 - work and school security part 24 - accessible security checklists part 25 - practice scenarios part 26 - quick reference part 27 - official security resources part 1 - the four core cybersecurity habits cisa's secure our world guidance centers on four simple habits. this manual expands them for screen-reader users. situation safer action recognize and report phishing do not engage with suspicious messages; verify independently and report/delete them. use strong, unique passwords use a password manager; do not reuse a password across accounts. turn on mfa use the strongest option offered; prefer phishing-resistant methods where available. install software updates apply security updates promptly from official update mechanisms. password length: cisa's current consumer guidance recommends passwords of at least 16 characters, random and unique for each account, with a password manager to create and store them. part 2 - what phishing is phishing is an attempt to make you open a harmful attachment, visit a fake site, reveal information, approve a login, send money, or install software. urgency: 'act in 30 minutes or your account will close.' fear: 'your computer has a virus.' authority: 'this is your bank, boss, police, irs, microsoft, apple, google, or it department.' reward: 'you won a prize/refund.' scarcity: 'only one item left; pay now.' secrecy: 'do not tell anyone.' payment pressure: gift cards, cryptocurrency, wire transfer, payment app, or cash. credential request: password, verification code, recovery code, pin, or remote access. screen-reader-specific warning: a link's spoken text can say one thing while its real destination is different. a sender display name can also be forged or misleading. always verify the actual address/domain when the decision matters. part 3 - accessible sender verification 3.1 verify an email sender what you will learn: check the actual sender address instead of trusting the display name. before you begin: do not reply yet. exactly how to do it open the message without activating links or attachments. move to the from/sender field. use your email program's message-details or sender-details command to read the full email address. spell the domain character by character if necessary. compare the domain with the organization's known official domain. if the message asks for action, leave the message and contact the organization using a known app, saved bookmark, statement/card number, or manually typed official website. what should happen: you know the actual sender address and have verified the request independently. if that does not happen: if your email client hides the full address, open message details/headers or use a different trusted client/device. do not treat a display name as proof. practice: inspect three legitimate messages and identify their full sender domains. 3.2 verify a caller or text sender what you will learn: do not trust caller id or the number in the message. before you begin: a call/text claims to be from an institution or person. exactly how to do it do not provide credentials or money. end the call or stop replying. find the contact through a trusted source you already possess. call back using the trusted number, not the number supplied by the caller/message. for family emergencies, contact the person or another family member through a known number. what should happen: you verify identity through a separate channel. if that does not happen: caller id and message sender names/numbers can be spoofed. practice: practice finding a bank or utility number from an official statement or app. part 4 - accessible link verification 4.1 inspect a link without opening it what you will learn: determine the destination domain first. before you begin: focus the link but do not activate it. exactly how to do it listen to the visible link text. use your screen reader's link-information command or the application's context menu where available. press shift+f10 on windows to open the link context menu. choose copy link address when available instead of open. paste the copied address into a safe text editor such as notepad. read/spell the domain carefully. cancel/delete the pasted text after inspection if it contains a personal token. what should happen: you can examine the destination without visiting it. if that does not happen: some tracking links are long or obscured. if the message is asking you to sign in, skip the link entirely and reach the service through a known app/bookmark/typed address. practice: inspect several trusted links and identify the domain. domain rule: read the registered domain, not just words anywhere in the address. a name such as bank.example.com.evil-site.test is controlled by evil-site.test, not by 'bank.example.com'. 4.2 use the independent-path method what you will learn: avoid link analysis when a safer route exists. before you begin: a message says an account needs attention. exactly how to do it close or leave the message. open the institution's official app, your saved trusted bookmark, or type the kn

windows and jaws users. all manuals ten focus lessons my progress identify your focus model first this course emphasizes the focus 40 blue fifth generation. a fifth-generation focus has a menu button centered between braille keys 1 and 4. older focus 40 blue models have different controls, ports, features, and firmware. never install firmware until the exact model and generation are confirmed. use the official guide for the assigned device generation. start jaws before connecting the focus to windows. save open work before changing connections or settings. use instructor-provided or fictional files during practice. never submit passwords, pairing codes, serial numbers, protected books, or private workplace information. major controls and features 40 refreshable braille cells: display one line of computer text in braille. cursor router buttons: move the cursor, activate links, and support text selection. perkins-style keyboard and braillein: enter text and windows or jaws commands. panning buttons, rocker bars, and nav rockers: move through text and structured information. usb and bluetooth: connect to computers and supported mobile devices. fifth-generation scratchpad and brf book reader: create notes and read supported files without a computer. basic and advanced how-tos connect the focus to jaws by usb keyboard commands: insert+j opens the jaws window. alt+o opens options, then b opens braille in common jaws versions. start jaws and save open work. connect the focus directly with its usb cable and power it on. wait for the braille cells to refresh. open jaws braille settings and confirm focus is the active display. press a windows key and verify that its result appears in both speech and braille. you should feel: text matching the focused windows control. if that does not happen: confirm the cable, power, jaws driver, and exact focus generation before changing settings. read, pan, and route the cursor device commands: the left and right panning buttons move one display width. a cursor router button moves the cursor to its corresponding braille cell. open a harmless practice document. read the current 40-cell line from left to right. press the right panning button once and confirm the next portion appears. press the left panning button to return. press the cursor router above a known word. type one practice character, verify its location, then undo with ctrl+z. if that does not happen: confirm the active window and editing caret before routing again. use focus keyboard help device command: press space with t-h chord, dots 1-4-5-6, for focus keyboard help. save work and turn keyboard help on. press one unfamiliar focus control. read its description without performing the command. exit help before returning to the document. if that does not happen: with focus connected to jaws, press insert+space followed by j and search jaws command search for the function. switch among saved connections device commands: on fifth-generation focus blue, menu+dot 1 through menu+dot 5 selects a bluetooth connection; menu+dot 8 selects usb. save work on the currently connected device. identify which connection number belongs to the target device. press menu with the assigned dot once. wait for the display to refresh and verify the target deviceâ€™s focused item. use menu+dot 8 to return to usb when needed. if that does not happen: do not repeat rapidly. confirm pairing and the saved connection number in the focus connections menu. ten-lesson learning path lesson 1: orientation, power, and device identification â€” create a tactile orientation guide naming the major controls and explaining how to identify the device generation. lesson 2: connect by usb and configure jaws â€” write a usb connection and jaws verification checklist. lesson 3: pair and manage bluetooth connections â€” create a credential-free bluetooth pairing and connection-switching guide. lesson 4: read, pan, route the cursor, and select text â€” submit a command chart for panning, navigation, cursor routing, and text selection. lesson 5: type with braillein and edit text â€” create focus-lesson-5.txt or docx containing a short corrected workplace note. lesson 6: navigate windows, file explorer, and documents â€” create a keyboard-and-braille workflow for finding and reading a workplace file. lesson 7: navigate webpages, forms, lists, and tables â€” document an accessible web-navigation practice session. lesson 8: use scratchpad, brf book reader, and microsd safely â€” create a local note and a storage-safety checklist; submit only your original note. lesson 9: braille settings, study mode, cleaning, and updates â€” create a safe settings, cleaning, and firmware checklist. lesson 10: final focus 40 blue workplace project â€” complete an end-to-end focus 40 blue workplace task and submit only the original summary. safe working routine identify the focus model and generation. confirm power, battery, cable, and connection mode. confirm the active jaws braille display and windows focus. practice on a copy and verify the destination before saving or transferring. restore reversible settings after practice. disconnect, clean, and update only according to the official instructions. official freedom scientific references focus blue fifth-generation user guide focus blue training and jaws features focus 40 blue lessons provide assignments and progress tracking when you want a course experience. basic 1: orientation, power, and device identification basic 2: connect by usb and configure jaws basic 3: pair and navigate webpages, forms, lists, and tables advanced 8: use scratchpad, brf book reader, and microsd safely advanced 9: braille settings, study mode, cleaning, and updates advanced 10: final focus 40 blue workplace project basic procedure 1. orientation, power, and device identification what you will learn: create a tactile orientation guide naming the major controls and explaining how to identify the device generation. before you begin: place the device on a stable surface, identify its exact model, and use only nonprivate practice files. save open work before changing connections or settings. buttons, nav rockers, rocker bars, selector buttons, and menu button by touch. use the centered menu button to identify a fifth-generation model; older focus models have different controls and firmware. when operating on battery, hold power for about two seconds to turn the display on. press menu to review battery status, then return without changing settings. hold power for about three and one-half seconds to turn off when not connected by usb. jaws and braille tip: use insert+t to confirm the window title, insert+tab to identify focus, and insert+1 for keyboard help. focus commands
